name: SH-7 Duophonic Analog Synthesizer
description: The SH-7 is an analog, duophonic synthesizer with 44 non-velocity-sensitive keys, built into the bottom part of a flight case and featuring an angled control surface. The SH-7 has two oscillators, both independently adjustable in foot (octave) range (2, 4, 8, 16, 32) and waveform (triangle, sawtooth, square, and modifiable pulse). Only VCO1 additionally provides a freely adjustable mix of square waves in 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 foot ranges. VCO2 can be synchronized to VCO1 or used when playing two voices on the keyboard. Mixable noise and a ring modulator complete the sound generation, which is shaped by a fixed high-pass filter and the dynamic VCF and VCA blocks. Two envelopes are available for this. Modulation can be done with the pitch bend lever, the LFO, and a random generator. CV/Gate inputs and outputs are also present, as well as an external audio input, headphone jack, and control input for the filter frequency.

description: The analog step sequencer 104 for the System-100 has two channels with up to 12 steps each. The number of steps is adjustable, and they can run sequentially or be output in parallel to control two synthesizer voices. The voltage range, adjustable with the controls, is selectable per channel between 2.5V, 5V, and 10V. Gate time and clock rate (tempo) are globally adjustable. The individual stages are referred to as steps. This sequencer established the brief series of Roland sequencers with directly adjustable control voltages for individual steps, i.e., the series of step sequencers. At the same time, the MC-8 was available, a sequencer whose steps were only programmable, not adjustable via controls.

name: TR-66 Rhythm Arranger
description: The TR-66 rhythm device is externally named 'Rhythm Arranger 66' and is an analog rhythm machine with 9 fixed rhythms selectable via push buttons and 18 additional rhythms selectable via a rotary switch, with each rhythm available in Variation A and B. Rhythms from the push-button group and the rotary switch group can be combined, and you can switch between Variation A, B, and an alternating AB sequence (called Auto), hence the nickname 'Arranger'. The Rhythm-Arranger 66 belongs to the second series of Roland rhythm devices, alongside the TR-330 and TR-700, and is built into a rectangular wooden case with controls on the front. On the back, there is a mono output for high and low levels and a connection for a start button, but no others. Tempo is adjusted via a rotary knob; synchronization is not possible. Selectable rhythms include Waltz, Jazz Waltz, Slow Rock, Bossa Nova, Samba, Mambo, Cha Cha, Beguine, Rhumba, Rock 1-6, Bass&Snare, Foxtrot 1-2, Swing 1-3, March, Parade, Habanera, Shuffle, and Tango.

name: US-2 Unit Selector
description: The Roland US-2 is a selector and splitter used to control two GR synthesizers (GR-100, GR-300, GR-700) either individually or simultaneously with a G-guitar (G-202, G-303, G-505, G-707, G-808, or guitar with GK-1). On the rear, there is one 24-pin input and two such outputs. On the top, there are two switches for outputs A and B, which can be individually turned on and off. LEDs indicate the switching status. Power is supplied via the 24-pin cable from one of the connected synthesizers. The US-2 can also be used for a G-33 or G-88 and two bass synthesizers, GR-33B or GR-77B. The US-2 is designed only for distributing a bass or guitar signal to two synthesizers and cannot, conversely, distribute two guitars/basses to one synthesizer. Mixed configurations of guitar and bass components are also not intended, nor is a combination with the BC-13. Therefore, it is not possible to control both the 13-pin and 24-pin systems simultaneously from one guitar via BC-13 and US-2.

name: Roland PS-2 Digital Pitch Shifter/Delay
description: The PS-2 Digital Pitch Shifter/Delay offers advanced pitch shifting and delay effects in a compact format.  A custom-designed LSI chip allows for pitch shifting over a full octave range (-1 to +1) with high speed, as well as pitch-shifted chorus, octave effects, and a variety of harmony effects.  For instant octave effects, the PS-2 includes preset +1 and -1 octave modes. A chromatic tuner (e.g., TU-12) can be connected to the Tuner Out jack to check the pitch shift amount in Manual mode. Metallic sounds are easily created by mixing the direct sound with the pitch-shifted sound up to +1 octave.  For a thick, full sound, mix the direct sound with the -1 octave pitch-shifted sound.  The PS-2 ensures clear effects even when playing chords.  For harmony effects, mix the direct sound with pitch-shifted thirds or fifths. The PS-2 can also be used as a high-quality digital delay, offering up to 2,000 ms of delay time.
